title: References, address-of, dereference, and pointers
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates understand aliases vs copies, how & and * actually work, and why raw pointers are needed to reach heap memory.

phases.goal: Establish that an lvalue reference is an alias, and that pointers store addresses as values.

must_hit.point: An lvalue reference is essentially an alias: a second name for an object that already exists, not a copy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says y bound to x names the same object/storage; changing either is visible through the other.

must_hit.point: A reference must be initialised when declared; an uninitialised reference is a compile error.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States int& y; fails because a reference must name something.

must_hit.point: A pointer is an object that holds a memory address (typically of another variable) as its value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines pointer as storing an address, and may mention raw/dumb vs smart pointers.

must_hit.point: A reference occupies no separate storage of its own; &x == &y when y aliases x.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the reference shares the object's address rather than getting its own box.

probes: What is an lvalue reference, and how does it differ from a separate copy of the object?
What does a pointer store, and how is that different from a reference?

hints.1: Think about whether a second name creates a second object.
hints.2: Contrast alias (same storage) with a variable that holds an address as its value.
hints.3: Reference = another label on the same box; pointer = its own object whose value is an address.

phases.goal: Show how &, *, const binding, temporary materialisation, and pointer init/deref actually operate.

must_hit.point: Unary & is address-of (returns the address of the first byte of the object); unary * dereference returns the value at an address as an lvalue; they are opposites.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains &x vs *(&x), and that * follows an address to the object.

must_hit.point: The meaning of & depends on context: after a type it declares an lvalue reference; unary in an expression is address-of; binary is bitwise AND.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the three roles of & with examples like int& ref, &x, and x & y.

must_hit.point: A const lvalue reference can bind to a modifiable lvalue; the object is treated as const through that reference but can still be modified through its original name.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through const int& ref { x } forbidding ref = 7 while x = 6 remains okay.

must_hit.point: A const lvalue reference binding to an rvalue materialises a hidden temporary on the stack; the reference binds to that temporary for the reference's lifetime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes rewriting const int& ref = 5 into a hidden temporary and binding to it; &ref is the temporary's address.

must_hit.point: Pointers must be initialised to a known value; an uninitialised pointer holds a garbage address and dereferencing it is undefined behaviour (wild pointer).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts int* ptr; with int* ptr3{ &x } and warns about wild pointers.

must_hit.point: Pointer use separates into declaration (int* p), initialisation with an address (p = &x), and dereferencing (*p).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three steps and keeps their syntax/roles distinct.

probes: Why can const int& ref = 5 compile, and what does &ref actually refer to?
Walk through printing x, &x, p, &p, and *p when p points at x.
How do you tell address-of & from reference & and from bitwise AND?

hints.1: Ask what physical memory backs a reference, and what unary * does to an address.
hints.2: For rvalues, mention compiler-created stack storage; for pointers, separate declare / assign address / dereference.
hints.3: const int& to 5 becomes a hidden temporary; p stores &x; *p follows that address; & after a type vs unary vs binary.

phases.goal: Contrast const vs non-const references and copying a pointer versus aliasing a pointer.

must_hit.point: Favour lvalue references to const over non-const unless you need to modify the referenced object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the preference for const refs when mutation is not required.

must_hit.point: Assigning one pointer to another copies the address into a separate pointer; a reference to a pointer (int*&) is an alias for the pointer itself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts int* p2 = p1 (independent copy of the address) with int*& p3 = p1 (same pointer).

must_hit.point: sizeof a pointer does not depend on pointee type; int*, double*, and char* are the same size (8 bytes on a typical modern 64-bit compiler).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says each pointer merely holds an address, so sizes match, citing 8 bytes on 64-bit.

probes: When would you choose const int& over int&?
What is the difference between int* p2 = p1 and int*& p3 = p1?

hints.1: One choice is about mutation rights; the other about copy versus alias.
hints.2: Const through the reference vs mutating via the original name; pointer assignment vs reference-to-pointer.
hints.3: Prefer const refs unless you must modify; p2 is a second pointer with the same address, p3 is another name for p1.

phases.goal: Explain why pointers exist: heap memory has no name and is only reachable by address.

must_hit.point: A program can access the code section and its own stack by name, but cannot reach heap memory directly by name because heap memory is requested at runtime.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls code/stack/heap and that heap blocks lack source-level names.

must_hit.point: A pointer on the stack stores the address of a heap block; dereferencing it is how the program reaches that anonymous dynamic memory (e.g. as a growing std::vector needs).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the stack-held pointer as the bridge to dynamically allocated heap storage.

probes: Why do we need pointers if we already have named variables on the stack?
How does a program access memory whose size or lifetime is only known at runtime?

hints.1: Think about which memory regions you can name in source code.
hints.2: Stack locals have names; heap allocations do not.
hints.3: Heap blocks are only usable via a stored address held in a pointer (often on the stack) and then dereferenced.

tradeoffs.topic: const lvalue reference vs non-const lvalue reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer const lvalue references unless you need to modify the object; a const ref can still bind to a modifiable lvalue but blocks mutation through that name, while the original identifier may still modify it.

tradeoffs.topic: copying a pointer (int* p2 = p1) vs reference to a pointer (int*& p3 = p1)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: p2 is a separate pointer that merely holds the same address, so reseating p2 leaves p1 alone; p3 aliases p1, so changing where it points also changes p1.
A reference is an alias that must be initialised and has no separate storage of its own; a pointer is its own object that stores an address, can be reseated, and is how you reach unnamed heap memory.

gotchas.trap: Treating & as always meaning the same thing.
gotchas.correction: After a type, & declares an lvalue reference; unary in an expression it is address-of; binary it is bitwise AND.
Dereference is unary; multiplication is binary — context distinguishes them.

gotchas.trap: Declaring a pointer without initialising it, then dereferencing.
gotchas.correction: An uninitialised pointer holds a garbage address (wild pointer); dereferencing it is undefined behaviour — always initialise to a known value.

gotchas.trap: Assuming const int& ref = 5 somehow takes the address of the literal 5 itself.
gotchas.correction: The compiler materialises a hidden stack temporary, binds the const reference to that temporary for the reference's lifetime, and &ref is the temporary's address (read-only through the const ref).

gotchas.trap: Believing a reference is a second object or can be left unbound.
gotchas.correction: A reference shares the referent's storage, must be initialised at declaration, and & of either name yields the same address.
